en: Inscription for the *Record of the Successive Patriarchs of Putuo*:
Although mountains and rivers are indeed established by Heaven and Earth, none fail to be transmitted and revered because of people.
If [the truth] were not transmitted and revered through others, consider this: throughout all time, the heavens and earth have remained the same;
throughout all time, the mountains and rivers have remained the same. Is it that Mount Song only came into existence after Bodhidharma, or that the Zhusi River valley never existed before Confucius?
Indeed, much is created by Heaven and established by Earth, yet there is much that remains hidden and never reaches transmission, and much that remains obscure and never receives reverence.
How could they be fully enumerated? All of these have not yet been transmitted through human intermediaries and thus hold great weight.
Mount Putuo rises preeminent above the sea’s edge, standing firm amidst the vast waters; as recorded in the Great Sūtras, it is the site where the Universal Gate manifests.
This is truly the site where successive patriarchs propagated the Dharma; it cannot be compared to ordinary scenic locales.
From the Song through the Ming dynasties, the Chan school flourished here in succession: Zhenxie led the way in the past, and Zufa revitalized it in the later period.
Before long, however, the world underwent its cyclical changes, and customs became ossified; for over a hundred years, the Dharma drum has not sounded. Alas! Forty...
The illustrious ancestral masters of former times have now vanished without a trace; who is to blame for this? I, being the unworthy descendant, have humbly assumed my duties on this mountain.

Fearing deeply that the virtue of our ancestors might not be exalted and that the spirits of the mountain might look upon me with disdain, I have sought among the various collections and examined the old records.

Indeed, regarding those who propagated the Dharma and served as abbots at this mountain, I have managed to recover a single phrase or a single verse from some, while from others I have obtained only...

Their names are all recorded in the *Shanzhi* (Records of the Mountains); however, there are occasional omissions in the canon. We await only scholars of profound and extensive learning to collect and supplement them.
This compilation has been re-carved to honor them, so that the countenances of the ancient masters of the fortieth generation may still be seen.
Written with reverent homage by the mountain-dwelling junior disciple, the śramaṇa Tongxu, on the middle day of the ninth month in the year of Bingzi,
the thirty-fifth year of the Great Qing Kangxi era,
for the *Record of the Successive Patriarchs of Putuo*.
Compiled by the Mountain-Dwelling Bhikṣu Tongxu.
Chan Master Zhenxie Qingliao (Successor of Danxia Zhi Chun). His title was Zhenxie;
his name was Qingliao. He was the son of the Lady Yong from Anchang in Zuomian, Shu. He was born with innate wisdom.

His faculties were prominent, his eyebrows and eyes were refined and elegant, and his spiritual demeanor was serene and profound. Upon seeing the Buddha, he felt such joyful attachment that he could not bear to leave him.

At the age of eleven, he relied upon Master Jun of Shengguo Temple to receive instruction. Furthermore, at the age of seven, he was tested on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and attained ordination. He received full precepts and began attending lectures.

He had achieved profound understanding of the sutras and śāstras, yet he considered verbal explanations to be ultimately not the final goal. Leaving the gorges, he traveled directly to the Mian and Han rivers to visit Chan Master Danxia Zichun.
Zichun asked, "What is your own self during the time of the empty kalpa? As the master was about to respond, Zichun struck him with his palm.

The master realized the essential meaning. The following day, Zichun ascended the hall and said: "The sun shines upon the solitary peak’s emerald hue; the moon descends upon the mountain stream, its waters cold."

"The patriarchs' mysterious and wondrous instructions—do not settle them within an inch of your heart. The Master stepped forward and said, "Today you cannot deceive me. [The Master] said, "Try to bring one up.
After the Master had been silent for a long while, Chūn said, "I thought you had suddenly awakened. The Master then departed.
He subsequently traveled north to Mount Wutai and the capital Bian, and south to Yizhen, where he visited Changlu Zu Zhao. Their words accorded in perfect harmony, and [Zu Zhao] commanded him...
He served as the attendant (*upasthāyaka*). For more than a year, Zhao shared his seat with him. As Zhao was habitually aged and infirm, he intended to retire.

He dreamed that someone told him, "A monk from Shu may take your place. Zhao did not yet know who this monk from Shu was. When the *xuánhuá* year *rényǐn* arrived and Zhao’s illness became critical, he suddenly recalled the previous omen.
The monk from Shu was none other than the Chief Seat (*śrāmaṇera*) Liao. He then entrusted the matter to the Imperial Envoy, Duke Chen, requesting that Liao succeed him on the seat. Long...
The "Reed-Flower Opening" (Lukai Fa) was used by him to repay Danxia Zichun with incense. He said, "Under Master Danxia, with a single blow of his palm, all my cleverness was exhausted;
I could find no opening through which to speak. Now, is there anyone who is so free and easy, yet not a man of ultimate penetration?
If there were not, each would be burdened by the bit and saddle. Thereupon, the Dongshan tradition flourished greatly.
The stream of Chan returned as if to its source. In the first year of the Xiaosheng era (the Xinhai year), the Master traveled south from Changlu and, crossing the sea, arrived here.
He built a hermitage on the mountain peak and named it "Solitary and Remote by the Seashore. Many of the outstanding talents of the Chan forest relied upon him.

The local administration petitioned the court to change the monastery from the Vinaya school to the Chan school. Using the skillful means of *aupaka* (compassionate guidance), he led more than seven hundred households throughout the coastal mountains; upon hearing his teaching, they were all transformed.

Yinju abandoned his fishing occupation; daily he saved the lives of thousands, tens of millions, and billions of creatures. Later, he was invited to succeed [the abbot] at Tiantai Guoqing and Xuefeng in Min.
By imperial decree, he was appointed to fill the vacancy at Yuyang Monastery, and by another edict, he was transferred to Jiangshan. He declined on the grounds of illness and did not go.

The following year, by imperial command, the two monasteries of Longxiang and Xingqing in Wenzhou were merged into a single Chan forest, and the Master was summoned to preside over it. Monks gathered there like clouds.

As his provisions of rice gruel were not sustained, the Emperor granted him one thousand *mǔ* of "Dharma-fields" (monastic lands) for his morning sustenance. Furthermore, by imperial decree, he was appointed as the abbot of Shuangjing Temple.

Empress Dowager Cining established Chongxian Temple for the Master to reside in, bestowing upon him gold-embroidered robes, silver, silk, and other ritual objects; the favor shown was exceptionally profound.

The Master considered this sufficient grounds to plan for his retirement. He ascended the hall and said: "To transform merit into the station [of realization] is the path of those who move forward. A jade hidden in the jing mountains..."
The mountain is noble; shifting positions to achieve merit is the very person who has returned. A flake of snow in a red furnace is spring.

When both merit and position are shifted, one’s entire being is free from obstruction. Letting go with no reliance, the stone woman ascends the loom at night; the secret chamber is empty and broomless.
At such a time, regarding this breathless phrase—how can you entrust yourself? After a long silence, he said: "Returning to the root, the wind drops the leaves."

The moon illuminates the empty pool to its depths. While he was manifesting illness, an imperial messenger came to inquire after his health; the Master responded with composed courtesy and expressed his thanks.

He then called for the Head Seat and said, "I am departing. He sat cross-legged, closed his eyes, and passed away. This was on the first day of the tenth month in the twenty-second year of the Shaoxing era, the Ren-shen year.
He had lived for sixty-two years and spent forty-five summer retreats in meditation. In total, he preached the Dharma in seven locations.

Fifth, he received an imperial edict sealed with purple clay, by which he was granted the ordination of four hundred disciples. Those who inherited his Dharma included more than thirty people, such as Zongjue.
His compiled *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) consists of two collections in several volumes that have circulated in the world. His words state: "To exhaust the subtle is to lose the root."
The essence is subtle and the fundamental source is lost; a single phrase cuts off the flow, reaching the ultimate depths of the profound abyss.

Therefore, where the golden needle is hidden, its brilliance is not revealed; when the jade thread passes through, it silently unfolds extraordinary colors. Although this is so, it still involves a mutual illumination of two aspects.
Furthermore, tell me: when skill and clumsiness do not reach it, how can one entrust oneself to it? After a long silence, he said: "Where the cloud-vines are exquisite, the green shade closes in;
the heights and depths of the crag-trees are locked in deep emerald. A monk asked: "If one does not fall into the traces of style, is it permitted to turn back?"
The Master said, "The path of the barren woman is not the same as that of those who toil. The monk asked, "What of the matter that transcends this?

The Master said, "Its subtlety lies before a single bubble; how could it admit the eyes of a thousand sages? The monk bowed. The Master said, "I only fear it is not so. The Master’s words and phrases were thus refined and subtle.
His spontaneous examinations and discernments were generally of this nature. This mountain school of Chan, in fact, originated with the Master.
He was acclaimed as the foremost in expounding the Dharma during his time.
He was Chan Master Zide Huikai (a successor of Hongzhi Jue);
his name was Huikai, his style name was Zide, and he was the son of the Zhang family of Kuaiji. From his youth, he severed worldly attachments and took leave of his kin to receive full ordination.
At Chengzhao Temple, he traveled alone with his single staff like a drifting cloud and met Changlu Zhenxie, from whom he believed he had attained some realization.

However, beneath the lightning-fast pivot [of Zhenxie’s teaching], he ultimately returned south. The monastic communities he encountered were like transient lodgings; he reviewed them once and abandoned them.
He then went to pay his respects to the Venerable Jue Hongzhi, whose majestic virtue was sovereign and whose reputation for the Way was preeminent in the age. Those who beheld him...
Everyone was struck with awe, yet Huí alone felt a burden in his heart; he did not rely on formal introductions but specifically requested to pay his respects at the Master’s seat.
Hongzhì gazed intently at Huí and accepted him. Huí harbored slight doubts as to why this was so, and thus he personally requested to be registered as a resident monk.
Hongzhi summoned Huì to his bedside and interrogated him regarding the "Treasure Mirror" verse. Huì hastily advanced with words, whereupon Hongzhi assumed a stern countenance and sent him away.
Huì then humbled himself in repentance, casting aside all his previous cherished attachments at once.

One night, while he was going before the sacred image of the Buddha to burn incense, Hongzhi happened to come forward; upon seeing him, Huì suddenly attained great enlightenment. From that time on, he asked...
The answer was without hesitation, and he received a prophecy of his future enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). In the *dingyi* year of the Xiangshu era, he began teaching at Putuo.
He sent word of his doctrinal expositions to Hongzhi, who was greatly pleased. His words were as follows: "The cold wind howls, sweeping the withered forest;

Leaves fall back to their root, revealing the bare heart. Ten thousand streams flow toward the source, the boat reaches the shore; The six windows reflect in emptiness, a mustard seed meets the needle. [This was] the original [verse].
Manifested and complete—do not seek it elsewhere. The nature-ground is vast and serene, shining through ancient and modern times.
Outside the door, the frost melts and the spring colors stir; the four mountains all join in the cry of wooden dragons. It is also said: "The nest knows the wind; the burrow knows the rain.
What is sweet is sweet; what is bitter is bitter. There is no need for calculation or deliberation. Five times five is naturally twenty-five. All manner of arrangements lead to this point.
"Ordinary. This is a phrase for those who have fully participated in the monastic tradition. Do you all understand it thoroughly? "The village elder knows nothing of the strength of Yao and Shun;

they beat the drum loudly to sacrifice to the River God. The spirit of the valley; the pivot of the gate. To investigate from the side within this realm, one returns to the path and attains the wondrous.
Though the clouds move, they are ever serene; though the moon is obscured, it shines all the more clearly. Guest and host intersect and interpenetrate—this is the state of true correctness.
He traveled extensively to various regions. When spring ended on the Ten Islands, the flowers withered and fell; the coral forests were bathed in the bright, blazing sun.

Thus, the style of Potalaka stood shoulder to shoulder with that of Tiantong. His relocation to Wanshou, followed by Xijiang and Xuedou, was all due to the earnest invitations of famous officials and high-ranking dignitaries.
In the *bingshen* year of the Chunxi era, he was summoned by imperial decree to head Jingci Monastery. In the *gengzi* year, he retired back to Xuedou.
On the twenty-ninth day of the second month of winter in the year of Gui-mao, at midnight, Xuedou bathed and passed away.
His entire body was interred to the right of the Mingjue Pagoda. His Dharma heirs were four: Huazang Huizu, Xuedou Deyun, Zhangxi Chongjian, and Xuedou Huan.
Followed by Chan Master Liao Ran (successor of Wuzhun of Mount Jing), Chan Master Bianzhi Lan,
Chan Master Xuewu Li, Chan Master Yuantang Yuan,
Chan Master Qu’an Cheng, and Chan Master Huan’an Chen.
Chan Master Jiange Shi, Chan Master Xiaohan Gao, and Chan Master Xianyun Deshao (who was a successor of Fozhao Guang). The master’s name was Deshao;
his style was Xianyun. During the Jiading era, he came to preside over this mountain. He petitioned the court, and ten thousand coins were granted to him.

Ming repaired and adorned the palace halls. When the halls were completed, the Emperor inscribed "The Precious Hall of Universal Penetration" (Yuántōng Bǎodiàn) and bestowed upon the Master the "Bridge of the Great Being" (Dàshì Qiáo).
He established Longzhāng Pavilion to enshrine them there.
Chan Master Dachu Pujie (Succeeded by Jingshan Yan):
The master’s name was Pujie; his style name was Dachuan. He was a native of Fenghua, Mingzhou. While presiding over the assembly, he cited the case of Master Muzhou:
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Muzhou said, "A troop of monks arrives; a troop of monks departs."
The monk departed. The verse says: A troop of patch-robed monks comes; A troop of patch-robed monks goes. Having smashed Muzhou’s barrier, Throughout the great earth, not an inch of soil remains.
Inscription on the Image of the World-Honored One Leaving the Mountains: With dragon-like markings and phoenix-like substance, he departs the royal palace.

Sleeves bared and robes worn through, he emerges from Snow Peak. His wisdom and vows shall surely empty all realms of existence; Yet one knows not when those realms of existence will be emptied. Master.
He once compiled the *Wudeng Huiyuan* (Compendium of the Five Lamps),
which has circulated in the world. [The records of] Chan Master Tiejiao Qing,
Chan Master Gurvan Zhuan, Chan Master Shenqu Huan, and Chan Master Wujiu Ji.
Chan Master Hanyan Wuzhuo was the successor of Chan Master Mengchuang Siqing. His name was Siqing;
his style name was Mengchuang. He was the son of the Yu family of Shanyin. Having completed his studies at Tianzhang Monastery in the prefecture, he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly.
Deshan would strike one upon entering the gate; Linji would shout upon entering the gate. Forcing a tortoise to form a pattern will never make it auspicious.
Here at Putuo, all is still and unmoving, yet it penetrates everything through resonance. Even a horse that lacks the power to travel a thousand li cannot truly chase the wind.
The Buddha ascends the hall for the occasion of his *nirvāṇa*. The Buddha’s true *dharmakāya* is like empty space;
why, then, on the fifteenth day of the second month, does he manifest every manner of death and life beneath the twin *śāla* trees? "Bamboo shadows sweep the steps, yet the dust does not stir;
the moon pierces the bottom of the pond, yet the water leaves no trace. Ascending the hall, [the Master] cited Master Baiyun Cunduan, who addressed the assembly, saying: "If Cunduan..."
[The Master] broke into a sweat once. The Master held up his whisk and said: "Do you wish to know where Old Man Baiyun has landed?
'Since undergoing fierce battles north of the Great Wall, I dare speak of battle formations south of the Yangtze. Ascending the hall, he cited Cao Shan’s departure from Dongshan.
Dongshan asked: "Where are you going, my son? Cao Shan replied: "I am going to the place of non-transformation. Dongshan said: "Non..."
"In a place of transformation, how could there be going? Caoshan said, "Even going does not involve transformation.
The Master said: "The clouds hide the seamless robe; the bird nests on the sproutless branch. Ascending the hall, he said: "The spring wind is like a blade; the spring rain is like ointment.
Where it cannot be cut or tailored, the color of the peach blossoms becomes even more exquisite. When Lingyun saw them once, he went away without doubt; Xie Lang’s dancing oars were even more so."
*Chengnao*: Entering the hall: Guizong chopping the snake, Bimozhe holding up the pitchfork, Heshan beating the drum, and Zhaozhou drinking tea.
Opening a shop on the crossroads of the city: buying and selling with cash, no credit allowed. Entering the hall: For thirty years I have sought a swordsman;
several times the leaves have fallen and branches have sprouted. Since first seeing the peach blossoms, [I have known him].
"Up until now, I have had no further doubts. The Master said, "In ordinary spring dreams there is nothing extraordinary;

it is only Lingyun who speaks of them to others. He continued, "As for what Xuansha said—'How perfectly true! How perfectly true!'—I venture to say that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate realization.

If one does not sleep on the same bed, how can one know that the lining of the quilt is worn through? Ascending the hall, he said: "Ten thousand miles away, not an inch of grass; atop the head, it is merely empty space."

Vastly. Stepping out the door is grass; beneath one’s feet it stretches on and on. Traveling by night, one merely covets the bright moon, unaware that one is crossing through water in one’s clothes against the cold.
—Master Shiwu Huan and Master Han’an Ju.
Chan Master Jishi of Songzhou;
Chan Master Riyue of Dongyan (the successor of Xiyuan Hui); Chan Master Qing of Hunxi;
Chan Master Gong of Baiyun; and Chan Master Zhi of Yuxi.
Chan Master Yong of Dongzhou (a successor in the lineage of Songyuan Yue under Shilin Gong), Chan Master Ning of Yishan, and National Teacher Zhibo of Japan initially visited the Master.
They set forth their reasons for seeking the Dharma, even to the point of weeping. The Master—

[The student] said, "In my school, there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma given to others. [The student] said, "I pray that the Master, out of compassion and skillful means, will provide an instruction.
The Master said, "From the beginning, it has been vast, empty, and pure; even compassion and skillful means do not exist therein."
Next: Chan Master Ciyuan; Chan Master Xianya Yu;
Chan Master Taixu Chong;
Chan Master Yuanfu Zhonghuai Xin (succeeded by Tiantong Tan).

The Master’s name was Huai-xin, with the courtesy name Fu-zhong. His secular surname was Jiang; he was a native of Fenghua in Ming. His father, [name], had once served as a school official in a certain county.
His mother, Lady Liu, dreamed one night that a large star fell into her chamber, emitting a light like fire.

She hurriedly picked it up and swallowed it; upon waking, she became pregnant. When he was born, his appearance was extraordinary compared to ordinary children, and his disposition was solemn and dignified, such that he never acted recklessly.

Whenever a śramaṇa came to his home, he would invariably leap up with joy and draw near to him. As he grew older, he received instruction in three scriptures from Dai Gong, a Jinshi of the Song dynasty;
although he fully mastered the essential meanings of these texts, they were not what he truly loved.
At the age of fifteen, he left home and followed the monk Zisi of Fahua Monastery, where he performed the duties of a novice. Subsequently, he shaved his head and became a full-fledged monk.

He received full ordination at Wutai Temple. Hearing that Master Quan of Banyan at Yanqing Monastery was propagating the principles of the Three Contemplations and Ten Vehicles, he went to associate with him.
After a long time, however, he sighed and said, "The scriptural teachings are so numerous that they are as vast as the ocean.

If one wishes to exhaustively master them, it is truly like counting grains of sand—merely a way to weary oneself in vain. He then abandoned his studies and departed, crossing the Zhejiang River to the west. Whenever he encountered...

Whenever he heard of a renowned monastic community, he would go there to seek instruction. However, the responses he received were mostly inconsistent with his own understanding, like two wedges that do not fit;

he could not overcome his frustration and indignation. He went to visit Master Zhuxi Tan at Tiantong. As the Master questioned him on his doubts, Tan perceived at a glance that he was a vessel for the Dharma, yet he treated him with a stern countenance and did not exchange a single word with him.
The Master’s many doubts grew even more intense. One day, during the ascent to the hall, [Tan] raised the case of Xinghua striking...
Regarding the "Ke Bin" (Subduing the Guest) kōan, he questioned the Master. The Master said, "How magnificent! You are a lion cub. Tan nodded his head in agreement.

From then on, Tan relied upon the Master, unable to bear leaving him, and was appointed to serve as the *weina* (rector). Not long after, Tan passed away. The Master summoned the assembly and requested that Master Xiu Yunwai be invited to succeed him in the abbotship of Tiantong.
The Master and Xiu would strike the rhythm together in their poetic exchanges; every beat was in accordance with the Dharma. Xiu often praised him for this.
It was said: "Master Xingong was a crimson banner of the Dong school and a white-browed elder of the Ji lineage.

In the Bingyin year of the Taiding era, the Xuanzheng Yuan requested that the Master come to reside at Guanyin Temple in Mingzhou. The Master exhorted his disciples, regarding every passing moment as if it were a foot-long jade disc, fearing lest they be lost.
In the Jisi year of the Tianli era, he moved to reside on this mountain. The Master did not [rely] upon his status or reputation..."

Chong emulated other mountains by decorating his carriages and increasing his retinue to show off to others. [The Master], however, carried only a single alms bowl and begged for food throughout the regions of Wu and Chu.
When the Prince of Zhennan prepared incense and flowers to welcome him to his residence, he humbly sought instruction from the Master.

The Master’s words struck at the very core of the truth, and the Prince further presented an image of Bodhidharma, requesting a eulogy. The Master took up his brush without hesitation; the phrasing was profound and far-reaching. The Prince—

He was deeply moved and filled with admiration. King Xuanrang also dispatched an envoy to present sandalwood incense and a purple *kāṣāya* robe, requesting instruction on the essentials of the Dharma.

The Master guided them according to their respective capacities and dispositions. As these two worthy kings were the foremost figures among the great feudal lords, they were the first to pay him the highest honors;

consequently, there were no princes or commoners who did not look up to him with reverence at the mere sight of his reputation. Offerings and provisions arrived in such abundance that they piled up. Among the products of Gusu was a rare and exquisite stone.
The Master then procured skilled artisans and constructed a thirteen-story stūpa for the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, which he brought back to海东 (Haidong, i.e., the Eastern Sea).

He established it so that those with faith might pay their respects. (As it was built through the donation of currency by King Sunnyang, it is also known as the Crown Prince’s Stūpa. The Imperial Son-in-law (Fu-ma-du-wei), Gini, served as the postmaster for the King of Goryeo.
Prime Minister Satun reported the Master’s journey to the Emperor.

By imperial decree, he was granted the title "Chan Master of Vast Wisdom, Wondrous Enlightenment, and the Great Teaching of the Treasure of Knowledge," along with a set of golden-embroidered dharma robes. The Master resided on this mountain for fourteen years.
In the first year of the Zhizheng era, the Renwu year, he stayed at Yongzuo Temple on Mount Zhongtianzhu. In the Yiyou year, he moved to Tiantong. One hundred...
He restored all that had fallen into ruin. The construction of the Buddha Hall was the most massive undertaking; he likewise demolished its dilapidated state and rebuilt it anew.

The Master established a pagoda at the ancestral temple on Middle Peak and resolved with deep emotion to spend his final years there. In the winter of the Jichou year (1349), the Office of Censorship for Traveling Inspectors submitted a memorial inviting the Master to reside at the Great Longxiang Jiqing Temple.
There he proclaimed the teachings of the Chan school; ten thousand ears listened intently as he expounded with ease and without constraint.
Yet the profound mechanism [of his mind] was naturally harmonious; both the small and the great were filled with joy and venerated him as their own kin.

He then drew from his private resources of robes and alms-bowl to repair the hall that had previously remained unfinished. During the reign of Emperor Yuan, political chaos broke out and the turmoil of war horses raged on; temple affairs grew increasingly precarious and distressed.
Yet the Master dwelt amidst these conditions with equanimity, not allowing even a single thought to trouble his mind. One morning, as he rose, he sought a bath with fragrant water.
After bathing and changing his robes, he sat in the full lotus position and said to those around him, "I am about to depart. You should all take it upon yourselves to uphold the Dharma;
you must exert yourselves with diligent practice. Having finished speaking, he closed his eyes. His attendant shook him and called out, "If the Master is going, then go!
Will you not leave behind even a single word to show people? The Master glared at him and rebuked him. The attendant called out again.
He did not cease. The Master took up his brush and wrote: "Throughout my life, I have acted as a matchmaker for others;

for seventy-eight years, I have leaked [the secrets]. This morning, I let go of my hands and depart; ten thousand miles of clear sky, a single flake of snow. Having finished writing, he closed his eyes again.

It was the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month in the year of Dingyou. He was seventy-eight years old, with sixty-nine years since his ordination. His coffin remained open for seven days, and his countenance remained serene.
As he was born, so too were those who came to pay him homage gathered in throngs. Incense and wax torches were piled up like hills and mounds.
On the first day of the ninth month, his body was cremated before Mount Jūpao (Zǔbǎoshān). His *śarīra* relics were as large as beans and as fine as sesame seeds, brilliant in five colors;
they grew in clusters even in places reached by the smoke. They were enshrined in precious jars, which emitted light from outside the vessels. His disciple Kāṇḍa...
At the foot of Mount Shou, he enshrined [the relics] within a palace and further erected a stupa above it.

He separately divided his fingernails, hair, robes, and sandals, enshrining them at Mount Taibai in Siming. By nature, the Master was serene and humble; a joyful radiance overflowed from his countenance. Throughout his life, he never offended others with displays of sensory indulgence.
If anyone committed an offense against him, he would simply nod his head in response. Nevertheless, his diligent cultivation of the Way was unsurpassed.

From his youth until his old age, he silently recited one volume of the Lotus Sūtra every day. Even when the summer heat was so intense it could melt gold and the winter cold so severe it could crack glue, there was not a single day he failed to do so.
On many occasions, he experienced the fragrance of lotus flowers filling the courtyard, so rich and pervasive that it was beyond comparison with anything of this world.
When the Ming troops descended upon Jinling, the monks dispersed in all directions, but the Master sat alone in serene meditation, his eyes not looking toward the four quarters.
Though soldiers stood before him in full force, there was none who did not cast down his weapon and bow. Emperor Gaozu once visited the temple in person to listen to the Master’s Dharma discourse;
admiring the Master’s pure and sincere conduct, he specifically renamed Longxiang Temple the Great Tianjie Temple. As for the temple’s arrears...

Regarding the grain held by the common people, he dispatched officials to collect it on his behalf. When the Master was about to pass away, on the day before his death, the Emperor was leading troops at Jiangyin and dreamed that the Master came to see him wearing a brownish-brown *cīvara*.
The Emperor asked, "For what purpose have you come? The Master replied, "I am about to return to the West to bid you farewell.
Upon returning, the Emperor heard that the Master had passed away (*parinirvāṇa*), which matched exactly with his dream. Greatly pleased, he issued an imperial decree.

The Inner Treasury was opened to provide silk and currency to assist with his funeral arrangements; furthermore, a master of geomancy was commissioned to select a site for the burial of Qi’s younger brother.

On the evening the reliquary was raised, the Emperor personally presented offerings and escorted the procession out through the capital gates. The degree of such imperial favor and honor has no equal in recent times.
That he stands towering as a teacher of gods and men for an entire era is due to nothing other than the fact that what is true is never false.
By not being deluded, one draws near to the Way of the Buddha. The Master’s *Recorded Sayings* (Wuyi Yulu) in five volumes circulates in the world.
Chan Master Guding Zuming (Diansi of Mount Jing) was named Zuming and styled Guding.
He was the son of the Ying family of Fenghua. When Yuansou was residing at Lingyin Monastery, the Master went there to seek instruction.
One day, he entered the room and inquired about the circumstances of Huanglong seeing Ciming.

Duan interrogated him, saying, "As for Zhaozhou’s statement, 'The old woman of Mount Tai has been exposed by me,' Ciming laughed and said, 'Is this an insult? You must tell me, which of these two elders was it?'"
"Are the points of application the same or different? The Master said, "A single pair of unperforated iron hammers.
Wenduan asked, "If one were to attain enlightenment directly beneath Huanglong, what then? The Master said, "It is also like a diseased eye seeing floating flowers. Wenduan said, "Not so, not so."
